docs.title: Pilot
docs.text:
Pilot is a modern web-based control system for the PAROL6 6-axis robotic arm. It provides an intuitive browser interface with real-time 3D visualization, timeline-based motion programming, and live robot control.

About PAROL6

PAROL6 is an open-source 6-axis robotic arm created by Source Robotics. If you're building or learning about the robot itself, check out:

  • PAROL6 GitHub Repository - Hardware designs, BOM, and assembly instructions
  • Official PAROL6 Documentation - Comprehensive guides for building and calibrating your robot

Pilot is a community-developed control interface that runs alongside your PAROL6 robot.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Real-time 3D Visualization - Interactive 3D robot model with live hardware tracking
  • Dual Control Modes - Joint space and Cartesian space motion control
  • Timeline Editor - Visual programming with keyframe-based motion sequences
  • Live Control - Real-time hardware following with trajectory preview
  • Tool Management - Configurable end-effectors with TCP offset and gripper support
  • WebSocket Streaming - High-frequency robot status updates

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: PAROL6 uses a single config.yaml file in the project root for all system settings.

docs.title: Serial Port Setup
docs.text: The most important setting is the serial port connection to your robot.

docs.title: Find Your Serial Port
docs.text:
# List available serial ports
ls -l /dev/ttyACM* /dev/ttyUSB*

Common port names: - /dev/ttyACM0 - Most common on Linux/Raspberry Pi - /dev/ttyUSB0 - USB-to-serial adapters

docs.title: Configure the Port
docs.text:
Edit config.yaml:

robot:
  com_port: /dev/ttyACM0  # Change to your port
  baud_rate: 3000000      # Do not change unless instructed

Serial Port Permissions

Ensure your user is in the dialout group: 

sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER
Log out and back in for the change to take effect.

docs.title: Robot Settings
docs.text:
robot:
  com_port: /dev/ttyACM0      # Serial port to robot
  baud_rate: 3000000          # Communication speed (don't change)
  auto_home_on_startup: false # Auto-home when commander starts
  estop_enabled: true         # Enable emergency stop
  j2_backlash_offset: 6       # J2 backlash compensation (degrees)
  timeout: 0                  # Serial timeout (0 = no timeout)

docs.title: Speed and Motion
docs.text:
ui:
  default_speed_percentage: 50        # Default motion speed (1-100)
  default_acceleration_percentage: 90 # Default acceleration (1-100)
  step_angle: 1                       # Jog step size in degrees
  cartesian_position_step_mm: 1       # Cartesian jog step in mm

Start Slow

Keep default_speed_percentage low (30-50) when testing new motions.

docs.title: API Server
docs.text:
api:
  host: 0.0.0.0   # Listen on all interfaces
  port: 3001      # API port

docs.title: WebSocket Streaming
docs.text:
api:
  ws_default_rate_hz: 10  # Status update frequency (Hz)
  ws_max_rate_hz: 50      # Maximum allowed rate

docs.title: Accessing from Other Devices
docs.text:
To access PAROL6 from other devices on your network:

  1. Find your IP address: 

    hostname -I

  2. Access the interface at http://<your-ip>:3000

The API is at port 3001 on the same IP.

docs.title: Camera Settings
docs.text:
camera:
  auto_start: false         # Start camera on system startup
  default_device: /dev/video0
  fps: 30
  jpeg_quality: 80
  resolution:
    width: 640
    height: 480

Enable auto_start: true if you have a USB camera connected.

docs.title: Robot Visualization
docs.text:
ui:
  hardware_robot:
    color: '#9096f4'      # Hardware position ghost color
    transparency: 0.3     # Ghost transparency (0-1)
  commander_robot:
    color: '#ffffff'      # Target position color
    transparency: 1

docs.title: Active Tool
docs.text:
ui:
  active_tool: duck  # ID of the mounted tool

See Tool Management for details on configuring tools.

docs.title: Saved Positions
docs.text:
Define commonly-used robot positions:

ui:
  saved_positions:
    - name: Home
      joints: [90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180]
    - name: Ready
      joints: [0, -90, 180, 0, 0, 90]
    - name: Shutdown pose
      joints: [90, -145, 108, 0, 0, 180]

Joint angles are in degrees, in order: J1, J2, J3, J4, J5, J6.

docs.title: Logging

logging:
  level: INFO              # Global log level
  api:
    level: DEBUG           # API-specific level

    level: INFO            # Commander-specific level
  file_output: logs/parol6.log
  stream_to_websocket: true

Log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This guide covers installing PAROL6 on your system. Choose between native installation or Docker deployment.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
• Robot: PAROL6 6-axis robotic arm with controller board
  • Computer: Raspberry Pi 4/5 (recommended) or Linux PC
  • Connection: USB cable to robot controller
  • Optional: USB camera for vision features

docs.title: Option 1: Docker Installation (Recommended)
docs.text: Docker is the easiest way to get started, especially for production use.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Docker and Docker Compose:

# Install Docker (Raspberry Pi / Debian / Ubuntu)
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Log out and back in, then install docker-compose
sudo apt install docker-compose

docs.title: Deploy with Docker
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/jointAxis77/parol6-webcommander.git
cd parol6-webcommander

# Pull and start all services
docker-compose pull
docker-compose up -d

That's it!

The interface is now available at http://localhost:3000

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
# Check all containers are running
docker-compose ps

# View logs
docker-compose logs -f

docs.title: Option 2: Native Installation
docs.text: For development or customization, install directly on your system.

docs.title: System Dependencies
docs.text:
# Update system
sudo apt-get update

# Install Python 3.9+
sudo apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv python3-dev

# Install Node.js 18+
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_18.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs

# Install PM2 process manager
sudo npm install -g pm2

docs.title: Clone Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jointAxis77/parol6-webcommander.git
cd parol6-webcommander
git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Python Environment
docs.text:
# Create virtual environment
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

Raspberry Pi OpenCV

If opencv-python fails on Raspberry Pi, use: 

sudo apt-get install python3-opencv

docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install
cd ..

sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
This guide walks you through moving your PAROL6 robot for the first time.

Safety First

  • Ensure the robot workspace is clear
  • Keep the emergency stop accessible
  • Start with low speed settings (30-50%)

docs.title: Step 1: Start the System
docs.text:
=== "Docker"

```bash
cd parol6-webcommander
docker-compose up -d
```

=== "Native (PM2)"

```bash
cd parol6
source venv/bin/activate
pm2 start ecosystem.config.js
```

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Interface
docs.text:
Open your browser to http://localhost:3000

You should see:

  • 3D visualization of the robot
  • Control panel on the right
  • Timeline at the bottom

docs.title: Step 3: Check Connection Status
docs.text:
Look at the top-right corner of the interface:

Indicator Meaning Green circle Connected to backend and robot Yellow circle Connected to backend, robot disconnected Red circle Backend disconnected

No Robot?

You can use the interface without a physical robot connected. The 3D visualization will show commanded positions.

docs.title: Step 4: Home the Robot
docs.text:
Before moving, home the robot to establish position reference:

  1. Click the Home button in the control panel
  2. Wait for the homing sequence to complete
  3. The robot will move to its home position

First-time Homing

On first power-up, homing is required to sync the software with actual joint positions.

docs.title: Step 5: Enable Live Control
docs.text:
Toggle Live Control in the top-right area:

  • When enabled: The physical robot follows your commands in real-time
  • When disabled: Only the 3D visualization moves (safe for testing)

Live Control

With Live Control enabled, the robot moves immediately when you change joint values. Be cautious!

docs.title: Step 6: Move in Joint Space
docs.text:
1. Ensure you're in Joint mode (toggle in the control panel)
  2. Use the sliders to adjust individual joints (J1-J6)
  3. Watch the 3D visualization update in real-time
  4. With Live Control enabled, the physical robot follows

Joint Reference:

Joint Motion J1 Base rotation J2 Shoulder (up/down) J3 Elbow (up/down) J4 Wrist rotation J5 Wrist pitch J6 Tool rotation

docs.title: Step 7: Move in Cartesian Space
docs.text:
1. Switch to Cartesian mode
  2. Adjust X, Y, Z position (in mm) and RX, RY, RZ orientation (in degrees)
  3. The IK solver calculates the required joint angles automatically

IK Limitations

Some positions may be unreachable due to joint limits or robot geometry. The interface will indicate when a target is invalid.

docs.title: Step 8: Use Saved Positions
docs.text:
1. Find the Saved Positions panel
  2. Click a position name (e.g., "Home", "Ready") to move there
  3. Save new positions by moving the robot and clicking Save Current

docs.title: Step 9: Adjust Speed
docs.text:
Use the speed slider to control motion speed:

  • 10-30%: Slow, careful movements
  • 50%: Normal operation
  • 80-100%: Fast movements (use with caution)

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Key Action E Emergency stop H Home robot Space Toggle Live Control ? Show help overlay

docs.title: Robot Not Responding
docs.text:
1. Check serial cable connection
  2. Verify com_port in config.yaml
  3. Check user is in dialout group
  4. View logs: pm2 logs or docker-compose logs commander

docs.title: Connection Status Red
docs.text:
1. Ensure all services are running: 
    pm2 status  # or docker-compose ps
  2. Check API is accessible at http://localhost:3001/docs

docs.title: IK Solver Fails
docs.text:
• Target may be outside robot workspace
  • Try a different orientation
  • Move closer to the center of the workspace

docs.title: Interface Overview
docs.text: This guide explains the main components of the Pilot control interface.

docs.title: Connection Status
docs.text:
Located in the top-right corner:

Status Indicator Meaning Connected Green Backend and robot connected Partial Yellow Backend connected, robot offline Disconnected Red Backend not reachable

docs.title: Live Control Toggle
docs.text:
• ON: Physical robot follows commanded positions in real-time
  • OFF: Only 3D visualization updates (safe mode for testing)

Live Control Warning

When Live Control is enabled, the robot moves immediately. Ensure the workspace is clear before enabling.

docs.title: 3D Visualization
docs.text: The central area shows an interactive 3D view of the robot.

docs.title: Mouse Controls
docs.text: Action Control Rotate view Left-click + drag Pan view Right-click + drag Zoom Scroll wheel Reset view Double-click

docs.title: Robot Visualization
docs.text:
Two robot models may be shown:

  • Solid robot: Commanded/target position (what you're controlling)
  • Ghost robot (semi-transparent): Actual hardware position from encoders

When both align, the robot has reached its target.

docs.title: Tool Visualization
docs.text: The mounted tool (gripper, etc.) is shown attached to the robot's end effector. Change tools in the control panel.

docs.title: Control Panel
docs.text: Located on the right side, the control panel has several sections.

docs.title: Mode Toggle: Joint / Cartesian
docs.text:
Switch between control modes:

=== "Joint Mode" - Control individual joints (J1-J6) - Direct angle input in degrees - Sliders for each joint - Shows current joint limits

=== "Cartesian Mode" - Control end-effector position/orientation - X, Y, Z position in millimeters - RX, RY, RZ orientation in degrees - Uses inverse kinematics (IK) solver

docs.title: Joint Sliders
docs.text:
In Joint mode, each slider controls one joint:

Joint Description Typical Range J1 Base rotation -170° to +170° J2 Shoulder -90° to +90° J3 Elbow -150° to +150° J4 Wrist 1 -180° to +180° J5 Wrist 2 -120° to +120° J6 Wrist 3 -180° to +180°

Joint Limits

Limits are enforced in software. The sliders won't exceed safe ranges.

docs.title: Cartesian Input
docs.text:
In Cartesian mode:

  • X, Y, Z: Position of tool center point (TCP) in mm
  • RX, RY, RZ: Orientation in degrees (Euler angles)

The IK solver calculates the joint angles needed to reach the target.

docs.title: Speed Control
docs.text:
Slider to adjust motion speed (1-100%):

  • 1-30%: Slow, precise movements
  • 30-70%: Normal operation
  • 70-100%: Fast movements

docs.title: Tool Selection
docs.text:
Dropdown to select the mounted tool. Each tool has:

  • TCP offset (affects Cartesian calculations)
  • Optional 3D mesh visualization
  • Optional gripper controls

docs.title: Gripper Control
docs.text:
If the active tool has a gripper:

  • Open/Close buttons
  • Visual feedback in 3D view

docs.title: Saved Positions
docs.text: Quick access to stored robot configurations.

docs.title: Using Saved Positions
docs.text:
1. Click a position name to move the robot there
  2. The motion uses current speed settings

docs.title: Saving New Positions
docs.text:
1. Move robot to desired position
  2. Click Save Current
  3. Enter a name for the position

docs.text:

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Important

Pilot controls a physical robot arm. Keep the workspace clear and stay alert during operation.

docs.title: Stopping Motion
docs.text:
• Click the STOP Robot button (appears during motion)
  • If your PAROL6 has a hardware e-stop, use it for immediate power cut

docs.title: Clearing E-Stop
docs.text:
1. Reset hardware e-stop if applicable
  2. Click Clear E-Stop in the interface

docs.title: Live Control
docs.text:
Live Control Warning

With Live Control enabled, the robot moves immediately when you change positions.

Before enabling:

  • Verify workspace is clear
  • Set speed appropriately (start low)
  • Be ready to stop motion

Safe practices:

  • Disable Live Control when programming
  • Preview motions with Live Control off first
  • Keep movements small and deliberate

docs.title: Timeline Programming
docs.text: The Timeline Editor allows you to create motion sequences by placing keyframes at specific times. This guide covers how to record, edit, and execute robot motions.

docs.title: Keyframes
docs.text:
A keyframe stores the complete robot state at a specific point in time:

  • All six joint angles
  • Timestamp on the timeline
  • Optional gripper state

docs.title: Playback vs Execution
docs.text:
• Playback: Preview in 3D visualization only (robot doesn't move)
  • Execute: Send the motion sequence to the physical robot

docs.title: Step 1: Set Timeline Duration
docs.text:
1. Locate the timeline duration setting
  2. Set total duration in seconds (default: 10s)

docs.title: Step 2: Add Keyframes
docs.text:
Method 1: Record Current Position

  1. Move the robot to the desired position (Joint or Cartesian mode)
  2. Position the timeline cursor at the desired time
  3. Click Add Keyframe or press the record button
  4. The keyframe appears on the timeline

Method 2: From Saved Positions

  1. Move timeline cursor to target time
  2. Click a Saved Position to set the robot there
  3. Add a keyframe at that position

docs.title: Step 3: Repeat
docs.text:
Add more keyframes at different times to create the full sequence.

Start and End

Always add keyframes at the beginning (0s) and end of your sequence to define the complete motion.

docs.title: Select a Keyframe
docs.text: Click on a keyframe marker in the timeline to select it.

docs.title: Move a Keyframe
docs.text: Drag a keyframe left or right to change its time position.

docs.title: Modify a Keyframe
docs.text:
1. Select the keyframe
  2. Adjust joint positions using the control panel
  3. The keyframe updates automatically

docs.title: Delete a Keyframe
docs.text:
1. Select the keyframe
  2. Press Delete or click the remove button

docs.title: Timeline Playback
docs.text:
1. Click Play to start playback
  2. The 3D visualization shows the interpolated motion
  3. The timeline cursor moves through the sequence
  4. Click Stop to halt playback

docs.title: Scrubbing
docs.text: Drag the timeline cursor manually to preview any point in the sequence.

docs.title: Executing on Robot
docs.text:
Safety Check

Before executing:

  • Ensure workspace is clear
  • Verify speed settings are appropriate
  • Preview the motion first

docs.title: Execute Sequence
docs.text:
1. Enable Live Control if not already on
  2. Click Execute to send the sequence to the robot
  3. The robot follows the motion in real-time
  4. The timeline cursor shows current progress

docs.title: Stop Execution
docs.text:
• Click Stop to halt execution
  • Press E for emergency stop

docs.title: Loop Variables
docs.text: For repetitive tasks, use loop variables to create patterns.

docs.title: Setting Up Loops
docs.text:
1. Define a loop variable (e.g., count)
  2. Set start value, end value, and increment
  3. Use the variable in your keyframes

docs.title: Example: Pick and Place
docs.text:
Loop: i from 0 to 3, step 1

Keyframe 0s: Home position
Keyframe 1s: Pick position + (i * offset)
Keyframe 2s: Gripper close
Keyframe 3s: Place position + (i * offset)
Keyframe 4s: Gripper open
Keyframe 5s: Home position

This creates 4 pick-and-place cycles with different positions.

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
Motion between keyframes is interpolated (smoothed):

  • Position: Linear interpolation between joint angles
  • Speed: Controlled by the speed percentage setting
  • Acceleration: Trapezoidal velocity profile

The robot moves smoothly between keyframes without abrupt starts or stops.

docs.title: Plan Your Path
docs.text:
1. Sketch the motion on paper first
  2. Identify key positions (start, waypoints, end)
  3. Add keyframes at each key position

docs.title: Avoid Singularities
docs.text:
Certain positions cause mathematical issues for the IK solver:

  • Arm fully extended
  • Joints aligned in certain ways

If you see jerky motion or errors, adjust the path to avoid these configurations.

docs.title: Use Appropriate Speed
docs.text:
• Slow (10-30%): Precision work, initial testing
  • Medium (30-60%): Normal operation
  • Fast (60-100%): Production speed (after testing)

docs.title: Add Buffer Time
docs.text: Leave extra time between keyframes for smooth acceleration and deceleration.

docs.title: Save a Sequence
docs.text: Sequences can be exported for later use or sharing.

docs.title: Load a Sequence
docs.text: Import previously saved sequences to replay or modify them.

docs.title: Jerky Motion
docs.text:
• Add more intermediate keyframes
  • Reduce speed
  • Check for near-singularity positions

docs.title: Robot Doesn't Match Preview
docs.text:
• Verify Live Control is enabled
  • Check connection status
  • Review logs for errors

docs.title: IK Errors
docs.text:
• Target position may be unreachable
  • Adjust the Cartesian target or use Joint mode
  • Check for joint limit violations

docs.title: Tool Management
docs.text: Tools (end-effectors) are devices mounted to the robot's J6 flange. Configure them in Pilot at /configuration.

docs.title: Creating a New Tool
docs.text:
1. Go to Configuration page (/configuration)
  2. Click the New button next to the tool selector
  3. Fill in the tool details:
Field Description Name Display name for the tool (required) Description Optional description Tool Type Static (fixed tool) or Binary (gripper with open/close)
  1. Upload a 3D mesh file (optional but recommended):
  2. Drag & drop or click the upload area
  3. Supported formats: .stl, .glb, .gltf

  4. Select Mesh Units (mm or m) to match your file

  5. Adjust the Mesh Offset to align the 3D model visually

  6. Set the TCP Offset to define the functional tool center point
  7. Click Create

docs.title: Mesh Offset (Visual)
docs.text:
Adjusts where the 3D model appears relative to the J6 flange. Use this to align your mesh visually with the robot.

Parameter Unit Description X, Y, Z meters Position offset from flange RX, RY, RZ degrees Rotation offset

docs.title: TCP Offset (Functional)
docs.text:
Defines the Tool Center Point - the reference point for all Cartesian movements. When you command the robot to a position, the TCP moves there.

Parameter Unit Description X, Y, Z mm Position of TCP relative to flange RX, RY, RZ degrees Orientation of TCP

The 3D preview shows a TCP gizmo (three colored arrows). Adjust the offset values until:

  1. The gizmo is positioned at your tool's working point (gripper tip, suction point, etc.)
  2. The gizmo axes align with real-world axes

Gizmo colors:

Gizmo Axis Orange X (Red) Cyan Y (Green) Magenta Z (Blue)

TCP vs Mesh

These are independent. Mesh Offset is purely visual. TCP Offset affects robot motion calculations.

docs.title: Configuring Grippers (Binary Tools)
docs.text:
For tools with open/close functionality:

  1. Set Tool Type to Binary
  2. Upload separate meshes for Open State and Closed State
  3. Configure Gripper I/O:
  4. I/O Pin: Which digital output controls the gripper (1 or 2)
  5. Open State: Whether HIGH or LOW signal opens the gripper

The 3D preview lets you toggle between open and closed states to verify your meshes.

docs.title: Selecting a Tool
docs.text:
On the main control page:

  1. Find the Tool dropdown in the control panel
  2. Select your tool from the list
  3. The 3D view updates to show the tool
  4. Cartesian coordinates now reference the new TCP
